- **Liver resection:** bleeding, bile leak, post-hepatectomy liver failure, hypoglycaemia, AKI, new coagulopathy and impaired lactate clearance.
- **Colorectal resection:** anastomotic leak, bowel ischaemia, prolonged ileus versus obstruction, stoma losses, VTE and pelvic infection.
- **Emergency bowel/liver trauma:** missed necrotic bowel or bleeding, compartment syndrome, open-abdomen losses, planned relook and ongoing shock.
- **Bariatric/reconstruction:** gastric staple-line leak, internal hernia, VTE, OIVI with OSA/OHS, flap thrombosis and pressure injury.

## 18.3 Nutrition, functional recovery and safe discharge

- Assess nutritional risk early; plan oral/enteral calories and protein rather than leaving the patient ‘nil by mouth until well’ without review.
- Enteral routes may include jejunal feeds after oesophagectomy or pancreatoduodenectomy; bowel viability/ileus/anastomotic concerns require surgical input.
- Monitor glucose, phosphate, Mg, K and thiamine in refeeding risk.
- Remove unnecessary vascular and urinary catheters, plan stoma education and mobilisation, review anticoagulation, analgesic route and opioid taper.
- Escalation instructions must specify red flags after ward transfer: new abdominal pain/distension, poor urine output, overt bleeding, tachycardia, fever or altered mental state.
- ICU discharge is not safe merely because vasopressors have stopped if a leak or wound complication is evolving.

## 18.4 A structured ICU problem list after GI surgery

**Day 0:**

- Record the operation’s actual anatomy, resuscitation, airway/ventilator and analgesic strategy, drain outputs and postoperative surgical escalation triggers.
- **Days 1–3:** review fluid accumulation, early AKI, respiratory complications, bleeding, infection, VTE prevention and early nutrition; recheck whether IV maintenance and oxygen remain necessary.
- **Days 3–7:** increasing vigilance for anastomotic leak, pancreatic fistula/sentinel haemorrhage, abscess, delayed bowel ischaemia and liver dysfunction.
- These are illustrative time patterns, not rules that exclude earlier/later complications.
- An ICU plan for an open abdomen must state relook timing, organ support, nutrition and losses.
- Every day ask whether worsening physiology reflects a new surgical problem rather than merely inadequate ICU medication.

- Prepare a structured recovery handover to ward: number/type of GI anastomoses, drain/ostomy plans, what to do if tachycardia or increased pain occurs, anticoagulation and catheter removals, nutrition route, antibiotic stop/review date, pain plan with conversion to oral drugs, mobility goals, delirium and cognition, and whether surgical contact is immediately available overnight.
- General postoperative guidelines cannot replace the specific surgeon’s reintervention thresholds and patient-level goals.

## 18.5 Postoperative complications: a diagnosis-driven escalation framework

- A day-1 tachycardic patient after major bowel surgery: examine pain, temperature, drains and stoma, fluid balance, blood loss, oxygenation and ECG; distinguish hypovolaemia/bleeding, pulmonary embolism, evolving sepsis, myocardial injury and postoperative pain.
- Transfuse based on clinical bleeding/oxygen delivery rather than an isolated number.
- A falling Hb with new abdominal distension warrants haemorrhage investigation; low urine output alone is not an indication for repeated 1-L crystalloid challenges.
- At day 3–7, new persistent tachycardia, fever, pain, ileus, confusion or vasopressor need may represent an anastomotic leak or collection; do not wait for obvious faeculent drain output.
- Discuss urgent CT with appropriate contrast and possible drainage or reoperation with the surgical team, while giving antibiotics/resuscitation when clinically indicated.

- Procedure-specific laboratory interpretation matters.
- After pancreatectomy, compare drain amylase and clinical condition, recognising the danger of delayed pseudoaneurysm bleeding after a fistula.
- After hepatectomy, monitor INR/bilirubin trends, glucose and encephalopathy along with lactate; impaired clearance is not a reason to ignore ongoing shock.
- After oesophagectomy, recurrent AF or hypoxaemia may signal leak or conduit ischaemia rather than simply a postoperative arrhythmia.
- For high-output stoma, measure the actual sodium/water and magnesium losses and use appropriate oral/IV replacement rather than indiscriminate hypotonic drinks.
- For prolonged ileus, exclude mechanical obstruction or abscess and rationalise opioids/electrolytes.
- Adapt nutrition, anticoagulation and analgesic route to functioning bowel and evolving coagulation.

Discharge from ICU must include an explicit contingency plan:

- What change in HR, oxygen requirement, lactate, abdominal signs, drain character or stoma output prompts an immediate call.
- Who may restart anticoagulants.
- How the epidural/peripheral catheter will be removed safely.
- How oral/enteral feeding and analgesia will progress.
- Who owns the imaging/reoperation decision.

- A short clinical handover that states ‘laparotomy uneventful’ without the reconstruction, ischaemia duration and leak risks is insufficient for an independent-specialist standard.
- The 2025 ESPEN surgical nutrition update emphasises early feeding where feasible and immediate identification of nutrition risk, particularly in major upper-GI surgery [R21].

items.title: 19. Organ procurement after neurological determination of death
items.body:
## 19.1 Ethical, physiological and procedural foundations

- The allocated outcome is **anaesthetic care for organ procurement in a donor declared brain dead** (donation after neurological determination of death, DBD).
- Do not confuse this with donation after circulatory determination of death (DCD), which has a distinct legal/ethical pathway, withdrawal process and warm-ischaemia timing.
- Before theatre confirm that death has been determined and documented by authorised clinicians under current legislation and ANZICS/local protocols, that donation authorisation and organ allocation are completed, and that the procurement team’s plan is understood.
- Anaesthetic involvement is **physiological donor support**, prevention of spinal reflex movement (if requested), ventilatory management and teamwork; it is not administering anaesthesia to a living conscious patient.
- Maintain respect for the deceased, privacy and family wishes, and document handover to mortuary/family teams.
- The current ANZICS Statement on Death and Organ Donation is the appropriate A/NZ governance source [R16].

**Brain-death physiology:**

- After a sympathetic ‘catecholamine storm’, loss of sympathetic tone can cause vasoplegia and low SVR; myocardial stunning may coexist.
- Diabetes insipidus from hypothalamic–pituitary injury causes polyuria, hypernatraemia and intravascular depletion.
- Poikilothermia, altered thyroid/adrenal axes, glycaemic disturbance and lung injury (neurogenic pulmonary oedema, aspiration, pneumonia) threaten graft quality.
- Organ-specific goals for oxygenation, cardiac output, preload, sodium/glucose, Hb and temperature are agreed with the donor ICU/transplant teams; fixed universal thresholds should not be invented.
- The preferred response to hypotension depends on vasoplegia versus true volume depletion versus poor cardiac function.
- Treat excessive urine output and hypernatraemia with fluid and appropriate desmopressin/vasopressin per donor protocol, monitoring sodium correction safely.
- Maintain temperature and prevent lung injury.

## 19.2 Theatre checklist and care before aortic cross-clamp

- Confirm identity/authorisations and organ list, expected sequence, airway/ventilator/vasopressors, vascular access, laboratory results (blood group, organ function, electrolytes, ABG), antibiotics and planned heparin.
- Maintain lung-protective ventilation and PEEP as feasible for lung procurement, avoid oxygen toxicity where possible while preserving adequate gas exchange, and communicate with retrieval surgeons if lungs are being recovered.
- Continue donor haemodynamic optimisation, check ionised Ca/K/Na/glucose, warming, perfusion and fluid balance.
- Large shifts can occur during dissection, sternotomy/laparotomy or venous manipulation; an arterial line and vasoactive infusions are usually useful.
- Spinal-mediated movements or haemodynamic responses may persist after brain death, and **neuromuscular blockade can be administered to prevent movement** in coordination with the retrieval team.
- Such reflexes do not establish consciousness.
- Some centres administer volatile agents for haemodynamic manipulation or immobility, but a conventional anaesthetic depth is not required for unconsciousness in a correctly declared DBD donor; follow donor procurement standards rather than a generic GA recipe.

- The surgeon may request systemic heparin and organ-specific perfusion preparation.
- Confirm timing of aortic cross-clamp, cold preservation solution and flush; coordinate with cardiac/lung, liver, renal and other teams.
- At cross-clamp and cessation of circulation, document time accurately; physiological support is discontinued when agreed.
- Avoid unnecessary delays that increase organ warm ischaemia.
- After retrieval, ensure respectful body care and clear documentation.
- DCD involves a **different** sequence with withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, observation after circulatory arrest, independent declaration of death and a mandatory stand-off period prescribed by local legislation/protocol; the anaesthetist must not conflate DCD with DBD procurement.
- A previous 2023 ANZCA SAQ on DCD is useful as contrast, not evidence that DCD is the content of SS_GG 1.11.

## 19.3 Donor-specific rescue: hypotension, polyuria, poor oxygenation

- If a DBD donor develops **hypotension**, re-evaluate actual circulating volume, haemorrhage/insufflation or surgical compression, vasoplegia and myocardial dysfunction.
- Give targeted fluid only if hypovolaemic/responsive and tolerating, otherwise use titrated vasopressors/inotropes.
- Persistent low output threatens kidneys/liver/heart even if MAP is restored by high SVR.
- With **large dilute urine volumes and rising sodium**, consider diabetes insipidus after brain injury; measure urine and plasma osmolality and replace free-water losses using donor-specific fluid and desmopressin/vasopressin strategy.
- Avoid rapidly changing chronic sodium without input from donation staff.
- With **hypoxaemia**, assess tube position, suction, recruit atelectasis judiciously and use lung-protective ventilation and oxygenation targets consistent with lung procurement.
- Notify the retrieval teams if an organ becomes unsuitable or perfusion deteriorates.
- The anaesthetist’s responsibility ends with properly documented physiological care and respectful completion of the authorised retrieval, not an independent decision about organ allocation or death determination.

## 19.4 DBD donor retrieval: practical haemodynamic and ethical boundaries

- The anaesthetist should independently verify documentation, not repeat or independently substitute for the legally authorised process determining death and consent.
- New Zealand and Australian protocols must be followed for death determination, organ authorisation, preservation and timing; an older checklist should be compared with the currently posted organ-donation forms [R22].
- After properly certified neurological death, spinal reflex movements and cardiovascular responses can still occur and may be managed with muscle relaxation/vasoactive agents; they do not imply preserved consciousness.
- Maintain a respectful environment and clear communication among retrieval, donor ICU, theatre and family-support staff.

- A practical donor physiological checklist includes haemodynamic phenotype (vasoplegia versus stunned LV versus true volume depletion), ventilator settings and oxygenation, fluid status, urine output/sodium and possible diabetes insipidus, K/Mg/Ca/glucose, temperature and endocrine support according to donor protocol.
- Use titrated vasopressor/inotrope therapy and targeted replacement rather than a routine fluid load that may injure lungs.
- Ensure antibiotics/cultures and blood results are transferred, and clarify whether the heart and lungs are being retrieved before accepting manoeuvres that threaten their function.
- Before cross-clamp, reconfirm heparin, vessel cannulation, cold perfusion solution and exact time documentation.
- Organ recovery and family/aftercare plans are multidisciplinary responsibilities, not routine anaesthetic emergence.

items.title: 20. Worked integration: the six decisions that separate an excellent answer from a generic list
items.los: Integrates the outcomes in this set
items.body:
## Case A — Unstable small-bowel obstruction with aspiration risk

- A 79-year-old with several days of vomiting, no stool, distension, K 2.7 mmol/L, bicarbonate 36 mmol/L, creatinine rising and BP 96/58 needs laparotomy for closed-loop obstruction.
- **Preoperative:** confirm suspected strangulation on CTA and whether source control is immediate; assess perfusion and ECG, place IVs, group/crossmatch and initiate guided chloride/potassium/fluid replacement.
- Correct dangerous hypokalaemia sufficiently for safer induction when time allows, but do not delay threatened bowel indefinitely; monitor Mg and repeat sampling.
- High aspirate volume despite fasting requires NGT decompression if safe and RSI with ETT, suction, preoxygenation and vasopressor plan.
- **Intraoperative:** monitor haemodynamics, perfusion, blood loss and bowel viability; distinguish simple adhesiolysis from necrotic bowel requiring resection/stoma.
- Ventilation may improve after decompression.
- **Postoperative:** replace measured NGT/stoma losses, correct ongoing electrolytes, watch for mesenteric ischaemia and infection; feed when anatomy and gut recovery permit.
- Do not overinterpret the metabolic alkalosis as a benign finding in the face of a strangulated bowel.

## Case B — Upper-GI bleeding with liver disease, sedation requested

- A cirrhotic patient is vomiting fresh blood with new encephalopathy and persistent hypotension.
- **Diagnosis:** likely variceal bleeding but ulcer and other sources remain possible.
- **Immediate care:** blood-based resuscitation, calcium/warming, vasoactive portal therapy plus antibiotics, airway and perfusion assessment and urgent endoscopist/ICU/IR coordination.
- **Airway:** active haematemesis and confusion favour cuffed intubation after preparing for a cardiovascular crash; deep sedation with an unprotected airway is unsafe.
- **Endoscopic management:** plan banding, secondary rescue if uncontrolled; distinguish restrictive stable transfusion from massive ongoing bleeding.
- **Post:** rebleeding, infection/aspiration, renal injury and encephalopathy.
- This is not a case in which a ‘routine gastroscopy propofol bolus’ addresses the risks.

## Case C — Prolonged robotic pelvic surgery with worsening physiology

- A patient in steep head-down tilt develops plateau pressure 34 cmH₂O, EtCO₂ 57 mmHg, facial oedema and MAP 58 during pneumoperitoneum.
- **Analyse:** elevated abdominal and intrathoracic pressure reduce compliance and venous return, while CO₂ absorption increases ventilatory demand.
- **Act:** communicate with surgeon to lower insufflation pressure/lessen tilt if feasible; verify ETT position, oxygenation, pneumothorax, subcutaneous gas and cardiac output; adjust minute ventilation safely and support perfusion according to cause.
- Review cumulative fluid/venous congestion and whether continuing the robotic position is safe.
- Before extubation assess airway oedema and respiratory reserve; prolonged head-down oedema means normal SpO₂ on ventilator is not adequate assurance.

## Case D — Partial hepatectomy with major venous bleeding

- During liver transection at requested low CVP, major bleeding begins and MAP falls.
- **Ask whether inflow is controlled:** Pringle manoeuvre controls portal venous/hepatic arterial inflow but not hepatic venous/IVC back-bleeding.
- Communicate immediately, support cardiac output and perfusion with blood-based resuscitation and targeted vasopressor, use calcium/warming and haemostatic monitoring, do not cling to CVP <5 during exsanguination.
- Recognise risk of gas embolism through open veins and monitor sudden ETCO₂/oxygenation change.
- After bleeding control, transition to measured fluid restoration and monitor postoperative hypoglycaemia, liver function, bile leak and coagulopathy.
- Epidural catheter management may become complicated by evolving thrombocytopenia and INR changes.

## Case E — Post-Whipple ‘sentinel bleed’ with tachycardia

- On day 6, drain blood changes from serous to red, Hb falls modestly and pulse is 115 despite a tolerable BP.
- Do not assume a small drain volume excludes major injury.
- Post-pancreatectomy fistula/infection can erode a nearby artery causing pseudoaneurysm; major haemorrhage may follow a minor sentinel bleed.
- Obtain immediate senior HPB/IR/ICU input, resuscitate, crossmatch, monitor serial Hb/coags/lactate, arrange urgent CTA/angiography or surgical control according to physiology.
- Avoid delaying with routine ward observation.
- Review anticoagulants and pain catheters.
- After control, monitor pancreatoenteric fistula, biliary sepsis, glucose and nutrition.

## Case F — Pancreatitis fluids cause respiratory deterioration

- A patient with alcohol-related pancreatitis receives repeated boluses because lipase remains high; after 24 h they have worsening hypoxia, bilateral crepitations and rising abdominal pressure despite MAP 75. **Reassess the hypothesis:** high lipase is not a volume target, and apparent pancreatic inflammation does not justify indefinite aggressive fluids.
- Examine haemodynamic responsiveness and congestion, repeat gas/renal function and fluid balance, assess for ARDS, fluid overload, cardiogenic cause or abdominal compartment physiology.
- Reduce unnecessary fluids, support ventilation and consider organ-support/diuresis when appropriate.
- Continue nutrition and aetiology treatment; avoid prophylactic antibiotics for sterile necrosis.
- WATERFALL supports harm from routine aggressive fluids in its studied population [T4].

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
- **T1.** [RELIEF — Restrictive versus Liberal Fluid Therapy for Major Abdominal Surgery (Myles et al., NEJM 2018)](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1801601). Population: approximately 3000 higher-risk patients undergoing major elective abdominal surgery, with perioperative restrictive versus more liberal IV fluid policies. Main finding: no significant improvement in one-year disability-free survival with restriction (81.9% versus 82.3%); **AKI was greater with the restrictive strategy (8.6% versus 5.0%)**. Application: avoid dogmatic zero-balance fluid treatment and protect renal/organ perfusion, while also avoiding overload. Limitations: studied planned major abdominal surgery in higher-risk patients, not uncontrolled haemorrhage, emergency septic laparotomy or liver resection; ‘liberal’ is not carte blanche for excessive fluids.
- **T2.** [OPTIMISE II — Cardiac output-guided haemodynamic therapy during major GI surgery (BMJ 2024)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39626899/). Population: 2498 older patients having major elective gastrointestinal surgery, assigned routine cardiac-output-guided IV fluid plus low-dose inotrope versus usual care. Main finding: no reduction in postoperative infection (23.2% versus 22.7%); early cardiac events/tachyarrhythmias were increased in the intervention group. Application: haemodynamic monitors may help selected high-risk patients, but a rigid monitor-plus-inotrope strategy is **not automatically superior**. Limitations: specific protocol and predominantly older elective patients; does not imply flow measurement is useless for every patient with shock or complex surgery.
- **T3.** [Villanueva et al. — Restrictive versus liberal transfusion in acute upper-GI bleeding (NEJM 2013)](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1211801). Population: acute upper-GI bleeding, restrictive Hb threshold around 70 g/L versus liberal around 90 g/L after assessment/resuscitation. Main finding: restrictive transfusion improved clinical outcomes, including survival/rebleeding in the studied population. Application: do not overtransfuse a stabilised UGIB patient, especially with portal-hypertension risks. Limitations: a trial policy is **not** a fixed trigger during uncontrolled exsanguination, and cardiac ischaemia or other patient-specific conditions may require individual thresholds.
- **T4.** [WATERFALL — Aggressive or Moderate Fluid Resuscitation in Acute Pancreatitis (NEJM 2022)](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2202884). Population: 249 patients in the interim analysis with acute pancreatitis randomised to aggressive or moderate lactated-Ringer’s regimens; stopped early for safety. Main finding: **fluid overload 20.5% versus 6.3%** with aggressive fluids, with no significant reduction in moderately severe/severe pancreatitis. Application: use moderated, repeated fluid reassessment rather than automatic large infusions. Limitations: excluded some very severe/advanced organ-failure presentations; a profoundly hypovolaemic or shocked patient still needs individualised resuscitation.
- **T5.** [HALT-IT — Tranexamic acid in significant gastrointestinal bleeding (Lancet 2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32563378/). Population: around 12,000 adults with significant upper or lower GI bleeding randomised to high-dose TXA or placebo. Main finding: bleeding death at five days was unchanged (≈4% in both groups); increased venous thromboembolism (0.8% versus 0.4%) and seizures. Application: **do not give routine TXA** for non-traumatic GI haemorrhage on the assumption that trauma results generalise. Limitations: evaluates a particular high-dose, prolonged regimen in GI bleeding; does not disprove TXA benefit in unrelated indications such as selected trauma or surgical bleeding.
- **T6.** [PANTER — Step-up approach versus open necrosectomy for necrotising pancreatitis (NEJM 2010)](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0908821). Population: infected necrotising pancreatitis, minimally invasive drainage-first with escalation versus primary open necrosectomy. Main finding: step-up strategy reduced major complications or death composite compared with routine open operation, while not powered to prove a mortality difference alone. Application: consider delayed multidisciplinary drainage/debridement after stabilisation rather than immediate open necrosectomy for every necrotic collection. Limitations: selected patients and available expertise; uncontrolled sepsis or compartment syndrome can necessitate earlier intervention.
- **T7.** [PONCHO — Same-admission versus interval cholecystectomy after mild gallstone pancreatitis (Lancet 2015)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26460661/). Population: patients recovering from mild gallstone pancreatitis. Main finding: same-admission surgery reduced recurrent gallstone-related events/readmission compared with delayed surgery. Application: plan index-admission cholecystectomy when clinically suitable once mild pancreatitis settles, rather than routinely deferring. Limitations: does not mean immediate cholecystectomy is safe during severe pancreatitis, persistent organ failure, infected collections or high surgical risk.

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Evidence audit and scope

The detailed workbook shows **17 parent LO rows** and **52 named components**. It labels **11 outcomes ‘COMPLETE THIS SET’ and six ‘COMPONENT THIS SET’**. The latter are completed elsewhere and are not falsely certified here. Chapter references indicate substantial worked teaching, not a one-line mention. Priority is exactly that in the latest workbook; it reflects study planning, not a College ranking.

**Allocation boundaries:** Urology, adrenal, gynaecology and renal-transplant complex surgery are reserved for Set 18 or other assigned sets despite being listed under the broader College SS_GG parent outcomes. The current workbook restricts this set to the named components above. In this set the general surgical problems are integrated with earlier ICU, airway and analgesia fundamentals; coverage of those broader parent outcomes is not falsely claimed.

Depth audit update (9 November 2026): the clinical subtopics that were originally compressed have been expanded within Chapters 2–4, 6, 8–14 and 16–19. Chapter coverage entries below should be read together with the corresponding new subsections. This crosswalk maps assigned content, not topics allocated to other sets.

## Linked references and source register

The sources below are grouped for efficient learning. A direct article link is provided in each entry. A journal abstract or landing page is **not** represented as proof of reading unrestricted full text. Contemporary guidance is preferred for recommendation thresholds; older BJA Education reviews remain valuable for physiology and procedural thinking. The current ANZCA curriculum and the uploaded workbook govern **allocation**, while published clinical resources inform **teaching**.

**Curriculum and general surgery resources**

- **R1.** [ANZCA Anaesthesia Training Program Curriculum — official trainee toolkit](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-trainee-toolkit). Source of curriculum and official examination-learning-outcome framework. The local uploaded v1.14 and Set 17 workbook rows were used for this document’s allocation; do not substitute an older public version.
- **R2.** [ERAS Society: Emergency laparotomy, Part 1 — preoperative identification, rapid assessment and optimisation (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8026421/). Best for simultaneous resuscitation, source-control urgency, analgesia, consent and risk appraisal.
- **R3.** [ERAS Society: Emergency laparotomy, Part 2 — intraoperative and postoperative care (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10241558/). Best for surgery-specific physiologic support, nutrition, fluid therapy and ICU recovery.
- **R4.** [ERAS Society: Elective colorectal surgery guideline (2025)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40783294/). Current perioperative bowel-fluid, analgesia, drains, nutrition and mobilisation recommendations. Read its population limits before applying to sepsis or perforation.

**Gastrointestinal haemorrhage, endoscopy and hepatobiliary diseases**

- **R5.** [ESGE: Endoscopic diagnosis/management of peptic ulcer bleeding, 2026 update](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42127996/). Current nonvariceal bleeding/endoscopy timing, high-risk ulcer techniques, recurrent bleeding and transcatheter embolisation guidance.
- **R6.** [British Society of Gastroenterology: Sedation in gastrointestinal endoscopy guideline (2023/24)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10850688/). Airway and ventilatory monitoring, high-risk procedural sedation and advanced endoscopy.
- **R7.** [Baveno VII: Renewing consensus in portal hypertension (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11090185/). Cirrhosis/variceal haemorrhage: targeted resuscitation, vasoactive therapy, antibiotics, early endoscopic and TIPS strategies.
- **R8.** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for minimally invasive abdominal and pelvic surgery (Carey, Jones & Fawcett, 2019)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807985/). Core physiology of CO₂ pneumoperitoneum, body positioning, perfusion, ventilation and patient access.
- **R9.** [ACG Guideline: Management of Acute Pancreatitis (2024)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38857482/). Diagnostic criteria, severity, CT timing, feeding, fluid resuscitation, antibiotics and biliary intervention.

**Complex procedures and ICU**

- **R10.** [ERAS Society: Guidelines for perioperative care in oesophagectomy](https://erassociety.org/guideline/guidelines-for-perioperative-care-in-esophagectomy-enhanced-recovery-after-surgery-eraso-society-recommendations/). Upper-GI cancer resection, respiratory recovery, nutrition and multimodal analgesia.
- **R11.** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for pancreatic resection surgery, Part 1 (Jarvis, Laing & James, 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11785549/). Pancreatic anatomy, preoperative risks and operation.
- **R12.** [BJA Education: Anaesthesia for pancreatic resection surgery, Part 2 (Jarvis, Laing & James, 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12190887/). Practical intraoperative and perioperative management, complications and recovery.
- **R13.** [ERAS Society: Perioperative care for liver surgery (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9726826/). Low venous-pressure resection phase, haemorrhage, temperature, balanced fluids and recovery; context-specific operative targets.
- **R14.** [BJA Education: Anaesthetic management of abdominal trauma (Edwards et al., 2025)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40083964/). Damage-control resuscitation and surgery, traumatic intra-abdominal bleeding and staged management.
- **R15.** [Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery: Acute mesenteric ischaemia management algorithm (2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12363320/). Time-critical diagnosis, arterial versus venous/nonocclusive patterns, CTA and rescue strategy.
- **R16.** [ANZICS: Fourth-edition Statement on Death and Organ Donation (official)](https://www.anzics.org/advocacy/death-organ-donation-dodc/). The Australian/New Zealand legal, ethical and physiological-care standard for deceased-donor retrieval, DBD versus DCD.
- **R17.** [ERAS Society: Bariatric surgery recommendations, 2021 update (published 2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8885505/). Respiratory/OSA management, anaesthesia, analgesia, VTE, feeding and micronutrient support.
- **R18.** [2025 European Society for Vascular Surgery mesenteric and renal arteries/veins guideline (PDF)](https://college-vasculaire.com/storage/page_paragraphe/25/page_paragraphe_fichier/68a731c50a3f1354579097d155973e1e.pdf). Current vascular criteria for mesenteric revascularisation and bowel viability assessment; complements the ICU gut-ischaemia chapter.
- **R19.** [ANZCA General Surgical, Urological, Gynaecological and Endoscopic specialised study unit reading guide](https://libguides.anzca.edu.au/anaestrain/ssu/general). Additional ANZCA library resource catalogue; articles are not all interchangeable or fully verified here.
- [R20. ERAS Society consensus review: Optimal perioperative care in breast reconstruction (2017). Supports normothermia, balanced goal-directed fluids, appropriate vasopressors, opioid-sparing analgesia and frequent free-flap surveillance.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9074892/)
- [R21. ESPEN guideline on clinical nutrition in surgery — update 2025. Applies to early nutrition assessment/feeding in malnourished surgical and major upper-GI populations.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40957230/)
- [R22. Organ Donation New Zealand: current donor documents/forms (reviewed September 2026). Local verification of death documentation, authorisation and procedural checklists.](https://organdonation.govt.nz/docs/documents-and-forms/)
- [R23. BJA Education: Anaesthesia for bariatric surgery (Reeve & Kennedy, 2022). Airway, respiratory reserve, OSA/OHS, monitoring and postoperative risk.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35614907/)
